{{other people||Frank Lewis (disambiguation){{!}}Frank Lewis}}
'''Frank Waring Lewis''' (August 25, 1912 – November 18, 2010) was an American [[List of cryptographers|cryptographer]] and [[cryptic crossword]] compiler.<ref name=NYT>{{cite news |url= https://www.nytimes.com/2010/12/03/arts/03lewis.html |title= Frank W. Lewis, Master of the Cryptic Crossword, Dies at 98 |last= Martin |first= Douglas |work= [[The New York Times]] |date= December 3, 2010 |accessdate=February 26, 2011}}</ref> His puzzles were printed in ''[[The Nation]]'' for over 60 years, for a total of 2,962 puzzles.<ref name=NYT/> [[Leonard Bernstein]], [[Kurt Vonnegut]], and [[Katha Pollitt]] were listed among the fans of his puzzles.<ref name=Nation>{{cite journal |url= http://www.thenation.com/article/156802/puzzlers-puzzler-frank-w-lewis |title= A Puzzler's Puzzler: On Frank W. Lewis |last= Long |first= Judith |date= December 20, 2010 |journal= [[The Nation]] |accessdate=February 26, 2011}}</ref>

==Personal life and career==
Lewis was born on August 25, 1912, in [[Salt Lake City]], [[Utah]].<ref name=NYT/> His father was from [[England]].<ref name=NYT/>

Lewis attended secretarial school and the [[University of Utah]], from which he later earned a degree in absentia.<ref name=NYT/> He passed the federal [[United States civil service|civil service test]], and earned a master's degree in music from [[The Catholic University of America]] in [[Washington, D.C.]]<ref name=NYT/>

In Washington, Lewis worked at government secretarial jobs.<ref name=NYT/> Just before [[World War II]], Lewis was approached by Col. [[William F. Friedman]], head of the [[United States Army|U.S. Army]]'s [[cryptography]] section, who was looking for "very smart" people.<ref name=NYT/> Lewis was hired as a civilian and helped break the code used to coordinate Japanese ships.<ref name=NYT/> After the war, he joined the [[National Security Agency]] (NSA).<ref name=NYT/> He was awarded the [[Decoration for Exceptional Civilian Service]] by both the [[United States Department of War|War Department]] and the NSA.<ref name=Nation/> He may be only person to have won two such medals.<ref name=Nation/> Much of his work remains classified.<ref name=Telegraph>{{cite news |url= https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/obituaries/culture-obituaries/8180268/Frank-Lewis.html |title= Frank Lewis |date= December 3, 2010 |work= [[The Daily Telegraph]] |accessdate=February 26, 2011}}</ref>

In 1969, he retired with his wife to the [[Caribbean]], but they relocated to [[Massachusetts]] after the eruption of the [[Montserrat]] volcano.<ref name=Powells>{{cite web |url= http://www.powells.com/book/cryptic-crosswords-from-the-nation-9781560258728/61-1 |title= Cryptic Crosswords from The Nation: About the Author |publisher= [[Powell's Books]] |accessdate=February 24, 2016}}</ref>

He died on November 18, 2010, at age 98. He was survived by his wife of 74 years, Sylvia (''[[née]]'' Shosteck) (October 7, 1915 - August 11, 2013).<ref name=NYT/> They had six children.<ref>{{cite news |title=Obituary: Frank W. Lewis |url=http://www.legacy.com/obituaries/wickedlocal-plymouth/obituary.aspx?n=frank-w-lewis&pid=146784084 |work= [[Old Colony Memorial (newspaper)|Old Colony Memorial]] |location= [[Plymouth, Massachusetts]] |date= November 23, 2010 |accessdate=January 31, 2012}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://obittree.com/obituary/us/massachusetts/plymouth/bartlett-funeral-home/sylvia-lewis/2000679/|title=Obituary: Sylvia Lewis|accessdate=December 17, 2020}}</ref>

==Puzzles==
Lewis discovered British-style cryptic crosswords while stationed during the war at the [[Bletchley Park]] code-breaking station in England.<ref name=Telegraph/> Lewis took over as ''The Nation'''s puzzle setter in 1947.<ref name=NYT/><ref name=PT>{{cite journal |url=http://www.psychologytoday.com/blog/in-practice/200804/homage-frank-w-lewis |title= Homage to Frank W. Lewis |date= April 28, 2008 |last= Kramer |first= Peter |journal= [[Psychology Today]] |accessdate=February 26, 2011}}</ref> When ''The Nation'' started running his puzzles every other week instead of weekly starting in 2008, the public outcry was so great it resumed printing the puzzles weekly.<ref name=NYT/><ref name=PT/> Lewis published his last puzzle in ''The Nation'' in December 2009, after which the magazine began reprinting old ones.<ref name=NYT/> After Lewis's death, the magazine continued to reprint old puzzles while it searched for a new puzzle setter.<ref name=NYT/>
